transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, doctor. Thanks for seeing me. I guess what made me come in is that... well, the things that usually make me feel like myself just started feeling really flat and heavy lately. Like my photography walks, for instance. I usually go out every Sunday. I actually still shoot on 35mm film, which is getting incredibly expensive to develop these days. The lab I use downtown just raised their prices again last month, and the guy who runs it—Frank, I think his name is, or maybe Fred—he was telling me it's because of all these supply chain issues with the silver halide chemicals. It's a whole ordeal just to get a roll of Kodak Gold processed now. 

But anyway... yeah, the photography, and mentoring the kids at the youth center... even just keeping a clean calendar at work. I'm an executive assistant, so my whole life is color-coded calendars, you know? But recently, I just... I stopped initiating any of it. It all just feels too heavy to even start.
Have you experienced periods like this before—where your interest in activities dropped and everything felt heavy—or is this the first time this has happened to you?

Well, let's see... it hasn't always been like this, no. But it's been going on for a while now. I'd say about a year and three months? Yeah, that sounds right. It all started right around the time my brother's health took a turn, and his behavior got really... unpredictable. I ended up having to take on a lot more coordination for him, dealing with his doctors and his apartment manager. Which, by the way, is a nightmare. Have you ever tried to get a straight answer out of a property management company? It's like talking to a brick wall. They have this online portal system that is supposed to make maintenance requests easier, but it just sends your message into a black hole. I swear I submitted three tickets about his leaky faucet before anyone even called me back, and even then, it was just an automated message. I had to threaten to withhold rent just to get a plumber out there, and the plumber they sent didn't even have the right tools! He showed up with a wrench that was too big and said he'd have to come back the next day. It's just exhausting, dealing with incompetence on that level when you're already stressed out, you know? But yeah, that's when this whole heavy feeling really started to set in, when I was managing all of that on top of my own life.
Before this started about 14 months ago, had you ever experienced a period lasting at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in things the way you're describing now?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I've had bad days, sure, but nothing that lasted two weeks like this. Before all this started with my brother, I was actually doing really well. I'd just gotten this new desk chair for my home office—one of those ergonomic ones with the mesh back? It was a total game-changer. You don't realize how much a bad chair affects your posture until you get a good one. I used to get these terrible knots right between my shoulder blades, especially when I was color-coding the quarterly reports for my boss. He likes everything done in these specific pastel shades, which is fine, but it takes forever to set up the conditional formatting in Excel. I actually took a whole weekend course just on advanced Excel functions a few years ago. The instructor was this guy who used to work for Microsoft, and he had all these wild stories about the early days of Windows 95. He said they used to have these massive launch parties... but anyway, no, I never felt this heavy, flat feeling for weeks at a time before last year.

Over these past 14 months since your brother's health changed, has the heavy, flat feeling been constant the whole time, or have there been periods—maybe weeks or longer—where you felt more like your normal self again?

Well, it hasn't been completely constant, no. For most of this whole period, I've actually been cycling back into these... these stretches where I'm incredibly driven. Like, overconfident, almost? I'll barely sleep, and I just take on way too much. Even if some weeks are quieter, I always end up back in that high-gear mode. 

Actually, during one of those stretches last spring, I decided I was going to reorganize the entire physical filing system at the office. We still have these massive metal filing cabinets from the 90s—the really heavy ones that look like they belong in a bunker? I don't know why we haven't digitized everything yet. My boss keeps saying it's a security thing, but I think he just likes the aesthetic of paper. Anyway, I stayed late for like three nights in a row, color-coding thousands of manila folders. I bought this label maker—a Brother P-touch, the one with the QWERTY keyboard—and I went through six cartridges of tape. The tape isn't cheap either, especially the laminated kind that doesn't peel off when the humidity gets high. Our office building has terrible climate control. In August, it feels like a swamp in there, and then by November, you're wearing a parka at your desk. They say they're going to upgrade the HVAC system, but they've been saying that since 2018. 

But yeah, I'd have these periods where I just felt like I could conquer the world on three hours of sleep, and then eventually, I'd crash back into that heavy, flat feeling again.

During those stretches where you felt overconfident and barely slept—like when you were reorganizing the filing system—did you experience anything unusual like hearing voices, seeing things, or having beliefs that others around you thought were strange? Or did anyone express serious concern about your behavior during those times?

Well, yeah, actually... when I get into those high-energy stretches, running on, you know, barely any sleep, things do get a little... intense. Like, I get this overwhelming certainty that the way things are arranged—like calendar problems or emails bouncing back—they mean something special. Like there's a hidden message just for me. And sometimes, when I'm really pushing it and not sleeping, I'll hear these... short comments. Just quick voices, like someone is right there, commenting on what I'm doing. 

It's actually kind of like how our office intercom system used to act up. Have I told you about that? We have this ancient system from the 80s, the kind with the little plastic buttons that light up amber when someone is paging you. For a while, it was picking up interference from a local radio station, I swear. You'd be sitting there trying to draft an agenda for the board meeting, and suddenly you'd hear the faint sound of a used car commercial coming through the speaker on your phone. My boss thought I was making it up until he heard it himself during a conference call with the regional director. The director was not amused, let me tell you. He's this very stern guy who wears suspenders every day—like, who wears suspenders anymore unless you're a lumberjack or a hipster? Anyway, we had to get the telecom guy out there, and he spent four hours in the server closet just to tell us the wiring was unshielded. Typical. But yeah, during those high stretches, the feeling about the messages gets really strong, and I do hear those little comments sometimes.

When you're in one of those high-energy stretches where you barely sleep and feel overconfident, how long do those periods typically last before you crash back into the heavy, flat feeling? Are we talking days, weeks, or longer?

Well, those elevated, driven stretches... the ones where I'm not sleeping much and feeling like I can take on the world, they've been coming back around for about eleven months now. It's like a cycle, you know? 

Speaking of cycles, my washing machine at home has been stuck on the spin cycle for weeks. It's a front-loader. Everyone said front-loaders were the way to go—better for the environment, uses less water, all that. But honestly, the rubber gasket around the door gets so gross if you don't wipe it down after every single load. Who has time for that? I tried using this special washing machine cleaner—affresh, I think it's called? It comes in these little tablets that look like giant mints. You just toss one in on a hot cycle. But it didn't fix the spinning issue. The repair guy said the control board is fried, and it would cost almost as much to fix it as it would to just buy a new machine. It's so frustrating how appliances are basically disposable these days. Remember when things used to last twenty years? My grandmother had this avocado green refrigerator that ran perfectly from 1974 until she moved into assisted living. But anyway, yeah, those high-energy periods have been recurring for about eleven months.
